Trying to Conceive

How Long Does It Usually Take to Get Pregnant?

Updated: July 1, 2026

This article is shown in English while its translation is prepared.

One of the most common questions when trying to conceive is simply: how long should this take? Understanding typical timelines can ease a lot of anxiety and help you know when patience is appropriate and when to seek advice.

The typical timeline

For most healthy couples having regular unprotected intercourse, a large share conceive within six months, and the majority within a year. Only a minority conceive in the very first month.

In other words, taking several months is completely normal and not a sign anything is wrong.

What affects how long it takes

Age is the biggest single factor, especially for the female partner, as both egg quantity and quality gradually decline with time. Overall health, weight, smoking, alcohol, and how well intercourse is timed to the fertile window also matter.

Underlying conditions — such as irregular ovulation, endometriosis, or male-factor issues — can extend the timeline.

Improving your odds each cycle

Timing intercourse to the fertile window (roughly the five days before and including ovulation) is the highest-impact thing you can do. Having intercourse every one to two days across that window works well.

Healthy habits for both partners, a prenatal vitamin with folic acid, and reducing stress where you can all support the process.

When to seek help

General guidance is to see a healthcare provider after about 12 months of trying without success — or after 6 months if the female partner is over 35, because time matters more with age.

Seek advice sooner if you have very irregular or absent periods, known reproductive conditions, or a history that concerns you.

Key takeaways

  • Most couples conceive within a year; many within six months.
  • Conceiving in the first month is the exception, not the rule.
  • Age is the biggest factor, along with health, weight, and timing.
  • Timing intercourse to the fertile window most improves your odds.
  • Seek help after 12 months trying — or 6 months if over 35.

Frequently asked questions

Is it normal to not conceive in the first few months?

Yes, entirely. Most couples take several months, and conceiving right away is less common than people expect.

Does age really make that much difference?

It does, particularly for the female partner, since fertility gradually declines with age. That is why the recommended time before seeking help is shorter after 35.

Can stress stop me getting pregnant?

Severe stress can affect cycles, but everyday stress is unlikely to prevent conception. Managing stress is still worthwhile for your wellbeing.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
